title: Dry January: Benefits, How to Do It, and What Happens After
excerpt: What Dry January is, what the research says about its benefits for sleep, liver, blood pressure, and your wallet, a week-by-week plan, and how to handle February.
metaDescription: Dry January explained: real benefits for sleep, liver, blood pressure and money, a week-by-week plan, and how to handle drinking again in February.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**Dry January is a one-month break from alcohol, from January 1 to January 31.** For most people who drink socially, it's one of the easiest ways to find out how alcohol actually affects your sleep, mood, weight, and wallet. Research on people who take part points to real but modest benefits: better sleep, more energy, lower blood pressure in regular drinkers, money saved, and, for many, drinking less in the months that follow. It works best when you plan for the tricky moments, and it's most useful when you use February to decide how you want to drink going forward.

This guide covers what Dry January is, what the evidence says it does (and doesn't do), a practical week-by-week plan, and how to come out of it without undoing the progress.

> **A quick safety note before you start.** Dry January is meant for people who drink socially and want a reset. It is not a way to manage alcohol dependence. **If you drink heavily every day, or you get shaky, sweaty, anxious, nauseous, or unable to sleep when you skip a drink, do not stop suddenly on your own.** Alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and, in rare cases, a dangerous condition called delirium tremens. Talk to a doctor first. They can help you cut down safely, sometimes with medication. In the US, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) is free and confidential. If someone has a seizure, is very confused, or is seeing things that aren't there after stopping drinking, call 911.

## What Is Dry January?

Dry January began as a public health campaign from the UK charity Alcohol Change UK, which was called Alcohol Concern when it launched the first official campaign in 2013. The idea was simple: after the heavy drinking of the holiday season, take a month off and see how you feel. It has since spread well beyond the UK. Plenty of people in the US, Canada, Australia, and elsewhere now do it every year, often alongside friends or coworkers.

A few things make it different from "quitting drinking":

- **It has an end date.** You commit to 31 days, not forever. That makes it feel doable, and it lowers the stakes if you're unsure.
- **It's an experiment, not a label.** You're not saying you have a problem. You're collecting information about how alcohol fits into your life.
- **It's social.** Because so many people do it at once, it's easier to say "I'm doing Dry January" than to explain why you're not drinking on a random Tuesday in March.

Dry January fits into a wider shift sometimes called moderation culture or mindful drinking. If you like the idea of questioning your drinking habits without committing to anything permanent, our guide to [being sober curious](/never-hungover/sober-curious) covers that mindset in more depth. And if a full month off feels like too much, [damp drinking](/never-hungover/damp-drinking) (cutting back rather than quitting) is a middle path many people use instead.

## What the Evidence Says About the Benefits

It's worth being clear about the quality of the evidence. Most research on Dry January comes from surveys of people who chose to take part, plus a handful of small clinical studies. That means the people studied were motivated, and some of the benefits they report could come from other changes they made at the same time, like eating better or exercising more in January. Still, the findings point in a consistent direction, and they fit with what we know about how alcohol affects the body.

### Better sleep

This is the benefit people mention most often, and it makes sense biologically. Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster, but it disrupts sleep later in the night. It suppresses REM sleep (the dreaming stage tied to memory and mood) in the first part of the night, then causes a rebound of lighter, broken sleep as your body clears the alcohol. Many people also wake up to use the bathroom or wake up hot and restless in the early hours.

Take alcohol out of the picture and those disruptions go away. Surveys of Dry January participants, run by researchers at the University of Sussex with Alcohol Change UK, have consistently found that a majority report sleeping better by the end of the month. If you want the detail on what alcohol does to each sleep stage, see our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025).

One honest caveat: some people sleep *worse* for the first few nights. If you're used to a drink or two before bed, your body has to relearn how to wind down without it. This usually settles within a week or so.

### Liver health

Your liver processes almost all the alcohol you drink. In people who drink regularly, the liver often shows signs of strain long before anything feels wrong. Blood tests may show raised liver enzymes (such as GGT and ALT), and fat can start to build up in liver cells, an early stage called alcohol-related fatty liver.

The good news is that early fatty liver is usually reversible, and the liver is good at recovering when it gets a break. Liver tests in regular drinkers often improve after a few weeks without alcohol. A month off won't fix established liver disease, and it isn't a substitute for medical care if you've been told your liver is damaged. But for a healthy social drinker, it gives the liver a genuine rest.

### Blood pressure, blood sugar, and weight

One of the most cited studies here was led by Gautam Mehta at the Royal Free Hospital in London and published in *BMJ Open* in 2018. It followed a group of moderate-to-heavy drinkers who either stopped drinking for a month or carried on as normal. The people who stopped saw improvements in insulin resistance (how well the body handles blood sugar), blood pressure, and body weight, along with lower levels of some growth factors linked to cancer risk. The study was small and the participants weren't randomly assigned, so the results are encouraging rather than definitive.

The blood pressure link is well established more broadly. Regular drinking raises blood pressure, and cutting back tends to lower it, with the biggest effect in people who drink more. Our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) goes into the details.

Weight changes are usually modest. Alcohol has about 7 calories per gram, nearly as much as fat, and drinks often come with snacks and late-night food. Cutting all of that for a month can lead to a small drop on the scale, but it varies a lot from person to person. Our guide to [weight loss after quitting alcohol](/never-hungover/weight-loss-after-quitting-alcohol) explains what's realistic and why some people see little change.

### Money

This one doesn't need a study. Add up what you'd normally spend on alcohol in a month, including bars, restaurants, delivery, and the bottle you pick up on the way home. Then add the costs that tend to come with drinking: rideshares, takeout, the hungover brunch. For someone who spends around $40 a week on drinks, a dry month is about $170 saved. For someone who goes out a couple of times a week, it can easily be several hundred dollars.

A useful trick is to move that money somewhere you can see it, like a separate savings account or a jar. Watching it build up is motivating, and it makes the cost of drinking more concrete.

### Mood, energy, and feeling in control

Participants often report more energy, clearer thinking, and steadier mood. Part of that is better sleep. Part of it is that you're no longer losing mornings to hangovers or the low, anxious feeling some people get the day after drinking (often called "hangxiety"). Our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains why that happens.

Many people also say they feel more in control of their drinking. That matters, because it's linked to what happens next.

### What happens in the months after

The most interesting question about Dry January is whether it changes anything long term. A study by Richard de Visser and colleagues at the University of Sussex, published in *Health Psychology* in 2016, followed people who signed up for Dry January. Six months later, on average, participants reported drinking less often and drinking less when they did, and they felt more confident about turning down a drink. Interestingly, even people who didn't complete the full month tended to cut back somewhat.

There's also a worry sometimes called the "rebound effect": that people will drink more in February to make up for it. The research so far suggests this is uncommon. Most participants drink the same or less afterward, though a minority do drink more. Later work from the same research group suggests the benefits are strongest for people who take part in the official campaign, with its support emails and app, compared with people who simply decide to have a quiet month on their own. Structure and support seem to help.

## Who Benefits Most From Dry January?

Dry January can be worthwhile for almost anyone who drinks, but it tends to make the biggest difference for:

- **People who drink most days**, even if it's just a glass or two. Daily drinking can creep up without you noticing, and it's where the health effects add up fastest. Our guide on [whether drinking every day is bad](/never-hungover/is-drinking-every-day-bad) covers what the research says about that pattern.
- **People who drink on autopilot**, such as a beer after work or wine with dinner, without really deciding to.
- **People coming off a heavy holiday season** who want a reset.
- **People curious about how alcohol affects their sleep, anxiety, skin, or digestion.** A month off is the clearest way to find out.

It's less suitable as a stand-alone plan for people who are physically dependent on alcohol. If you can't comfortably go a day or two without drinking, or you've tried to cut back before and couldn't, that's a sign to talk to a doctor rather than rely on a month of willpower. There's no shame in that, and a doctor can make stopping much safer and easier.

## How to Do Dry January Well: A Practical Plan

The people who get the most out of Dry January usually plan for it. Here's an approach that works for a lot of people.

### Before January 1: set yourself up

1. **Decide your "why."** Write down one or two reasons you're doing this. Better sleep? Saving for something? Seeing if you can? You'll come back to these on hard days.
2. **Clear the house, or at least move it.** If there's an open bottle of wine in the fridge, it's much harder to say no at 7 p.m. on a Thursday. Give it away, store it out of sight, or finish it before New Year's.
3. **Stock up on alternatives.** Find a few drinks you actually like: sparkling water with citrus, kombucha, tonic with bitters, ginger beer, or alcohol-free beer, wine, and spirits. Note that many "non-alcoholic" beers contain small amounts of alcohol (up to 0.5% in the US). That's fine for most people, but check our guide to [whether non-alcoholic beer has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol) if you want to avoid it completely.
4. **Tell a few people.** Saying it out loud makes it real, and friends are less likely to push a drink on you if they know. Better yet, recruit someone to do it with you.
5. **Pick a tracking tool.** The official Try Dry app from Alcohol Change UK tracks dry days, money saved, and calories avoided. Other apps do similar things. Our roundup of [mindful drinking apps](/never-hungover/mindful-drinking-apps) compares the options.

### Week 1: expect the routine to feel strange

The first week is often the hardest, not because of cravings so much as habit. The moment you get home, the first warm evening, Friday night: these are cues your brain links with a drink. Have a replacement ready for those exact moments. Some people find it helps to change the routine itself, like going for a walk after work instead of heading straight to the kitchen.

Sleep may be a little off for the first few nights. Keep a regular bedtime, avoid screens late, and cut back on caffeine after midday. It usually improves quickly.

### Weeks 2 and 3: the social test

By now the habit cues are weaker, but this is when the birthday party, work drinks, or a weekend away tends to show up. A few things help:

- **Have your answer ready.** "I'm doing Dry January" is usually enough. You don't owe anyone a longer explanation.
- **Get a drink in your hand early.** People are much less likely to offer you something if you're already holding a glass.
- **Plan your exit.** Social events can get less fun as everyone else gets drunker. It's fine to leave earlier than usual.
- **Suggest different plans.** Breakfast, a movie, a class, or a walk can replace the default of meeting at a bar.

This is also when many people start to notice the good stuff: waking up clearer, sleeping through, having whole weekends back.

### Week 4: notice what's changed

In the last week, take stock. How's your sleep compared with December? Your energy, mood, skin, digestion? How much have you saved? Did you miss drinking, and if so, in which situations? That last question is the most useful one, because it tells you where alcohol really fits in your life and where it was just habit.

### If you slip, keep going

A drink on January 14 doesn't cancel the previous 13 days. The research above found that even people who didn't make it through the whole month tended to drink less afterward. If you slip, ask what led to it, plan for that situation next time, and carry on. Some people decide to switch to drinking much less rather than not at all for the rest of the month, an approach sometimes called "damp January." That's still a meaningful change.

## What Happens When January Ends

February 1 is where Dry January either becomes a one-off or the start of a better pattern. A few things to keep in mind.

### Your tolerance will be lower

After a month off, the same number of drinks will affect you more than it did in December. You'll feel drunk sooner and the hangover can be worse. This is normal: some of the tolerance regular drinkers build up comes from the body adapting to frequent alcohol, and that fades with time off. Our guide to [alcohol tolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-tolerance) explains how this works. Don't try to "catch up" on your first night back.

### Plan your first drink

Rather than drinking by default on February 1, choose an occasion that's worth it. Eat first, drink slowly, alternate with water, and decide your limit before you start. It helps to know what counts as one drink, since restaurant pours are often bigger than a standard drink. Our guide to [what a standard drink is](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink) has the numbers.

### Decide what you want to keep

Many people come out of Dry January with a few rules they want to keep. Common ones include:

- No drinking on weeknights, or only on weekends.
- A set number of alcohol-free days each week.
- A drink limit for nights out.
- Keeping alcohol-free drinks as the default at home.
- A dry week or month at other times of year, such as "Sober October."

For reference, the US Dietary Guidelines suggest that adults who drink keep it to two drinks or fewer in a day for men and one drink or fewer for women, and they note that drinking less is better for health than drinking more. There's no level of drinking that's completely risk-free, but most of the harm is concentrated in heavier drinking.

### Pay attention to how drinking feels now

A month off gives you a clean comparison. If alcohol suddenly makes you feel worse than you remember, like groggy, anxious, or puffy the next day, that's useful information. Some people find they enjoy a drink more when it's occasional. Others find they don't miss it much at all and decide to keep drinking rarely.

### When to talk to a doctor

It's a good idea to see a doctor if you found Dry January much harder than you expected, if you had physical symptoms like shaking, sweating, or a racing heart in the first few days, or if you went back to drinking more than before. These can be signs that alcohol has a stronger hold than you thought. A doctor can talk through options without judgment. It's also worth asking for a liver blood test if you've been a regular drinker and want to know where you stand.

## Where Supplements Fit (and Where They Don't)

During Dry January itself, you don't need any hangover supplement, because there's nothing to recover from. That's one of the perks.

After January, some people who drink occasionally like to support their body on the nights they do. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers reliably or makes heavy drinking safe, and it doesn't change how much alcohol reaches your blood. It shouldn't be a reason to drink more than you planned. If you've decided to drink at an occasion and want to try it alongside food and water, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a well-reviewed budget option and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is our top-rated pick. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people use it. The habits with the best evidence for avoiding hangovers are covered in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Dry January is a 31-day break from alcohol that started as a UK public health campaign in 2013 and is now done worldwide.
- The most commonly reported benefits are better sleep, more energy, money saved, and feeling more in control. Small studies in regular drinkers also link a month off to lower blood pressure, better blood sugar control, and modest weight loss.
- Research suggests many participants drink less in the months afterward, even if they don't finish the whole month.
- Plan ahead: clear the house, stock alternatives, tell people, and have an answer ready for social events.
- Your tolerance will be lower in February, so plan your first drink and don't try to catch up.
- If you drink heavily every day or get withdrawal symptoms when you skip a drink, talk to a doctor before stopping. Stopping suddenly in that situation can be dangerous.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and public health guidance. Talk to a doctor if you have health conditions, take medications that interact with alcohol, or are unsure whether it's safe for you to stop drinking suddenly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is Dry January?**

Dry January is a month-long break from alcohol, from January 1 to January 31. It started as a public health campaign run by the UK charity Alcohol Change UK (then called Alcohol Concern) in 2013 and has since spread worldwide. It is a reset and an experiment, not a diagnosis or a promise to quit forever. Most people who take part go back to drinking in February, ideally with a better sense of how much and why.

**What are the benefits of Dry January?**

The most commonly reported benefits are better sleep, more energy, saving money, and feeling more in control of drinking. A small study of moderate-to-heavy drinkers at the Royal Free Hospital in London (Mehta and colleagues, BMJ Open, 2018) found that one month without alcohol was linked to lower blood pressure, better insulin resistance, and modest weight loss. Some people also lose a little weight, mainly from cutting liquid calories and late-night snacking. Results vary, and the biggest changes tend to show up in people who were drinking more to begin with.

**What happens to your body after a month without alcohol?**

In the first week, many people sleep a little worse before they sleep better, because the body is adjusting. By weeks two to four, people commonly report deeper sleep, steadier mood, and more energy in the morning. For regular drinkers, blood pressure can drift down and liver blood tests can improve, since the liver no longer has to process alcohol every day. A month won't undo years of heavy drinking, but it gives your body a real break and shows you how you feel without alcohol.

**Does Dry January help your liver?**

For many people, yes, at least in the short term. The liver handles almost all the alcohol you drink, and a few weeks off gives it a break. In people who drink regularly, liver tests such as GGT and ALT often improve after a period without alcohol, and early fat build-up in the liver can begin to reverse. A month off is not a treatment for liver disease, though. If you've been told you have high liver enzymes or fatty liver, work with your doctor on a longer-term plan.

**Is it safe to stop drinking suddenly for Dry January?**

For most people who drink socially or a few times a week, yes. But if you drink heavily every day, or you get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or nauseous when you go without a drink, stopping suddenly can be dangerous. Alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and, rarely, a life-threatening condition called delirium tremens. In that case, talk to a doctor before you stop. They can help you cut down safely, sometimes with medication.

**What if I slip up during Dry January?**

Keep going. One drink on January 12 does not cancel the 11 days before it or the days after. Many people find it helpful to ask what led to the slip (a party, a stressful day, boredom) and plan for that situation next time. Some people switch to a 'damp January' approach, drinking much less rather than nothing. The goal is to learn about your habits, not to pass or fail a test.

**Should I drink a lot on January 31 or February 1 to celebrate?**

It's better not to. After a month off, your tolerance will be lower, so the same number of drinks will hit harder and the hangover may be worse. Plan your first drink instead: pick an occasion you'll enjoy, eat first, alternate with water, and decide your limit before you start. Research on Dry January participants suggests many go on to drink less in the following months, and a planned first drink helps keep that going.
